source.title: The Normalization Method for Alleviating Pathological Sharpness in Wide Neural Networks
source.authors: Ryo Karakida; S. Akaho; S. Amari

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including supplementary material, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how last-layer mean subtraction changes sharpness and gradient-descent convergence across widths and learning rates; this differs from the claim version's benchmark accuracy measures.
record.gate_note: The paper studies random-initialized networks and reports FIM sharpness and gradient-descent training-loss results. It does not report classification error on CIFAR or other benchmarks. The cited claims about zero training error from prior work are not this study's results. Figure 2 and Figure S.2 show loss values by width and learning rate; the text gives qualitative conclusions but no recoverable per-cell values.
record.test_reason: The controlled gradient-descent sweeps test V6's learning-rate tolerance component using last-layer mean subtraction in fully connected synthetic regression networks. They do not establish faster accuracy gains.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially correct. More precisely, the authors conclude that last-layer batch normalization reduces width-dependent FIM sharpness under appropriate width–sample scaling, with mean subtraction providing the essential contribution. Their regression experiments show greater learning-rate tolerance; faster training is suggested rather than directly measured. Middle-layer batch normalization and layer normalization do not remove this sharpness in the analyzed settings.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes FIM eigenvalues and trains synthetic teacher-network regression models with full-batch gradient descent. Its normalization experiment uses last-layer mean subtraction, rather than the benchmark classification recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Last-layer mean subtraction changes the reported learning-rate convergence range; the authors say the larger convergent rates are independent of width. Results are shown for a single trial and for the minimum over ten trials.

fits_no_version.finding: Last-layer mean subtraction reduces the width scaling of initial FIM sharpness when sample count scales with width; middle-layer batch normalization and layer normalization retain pathological sharpness under the stated assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization placement and sample-count scaling determine whether normalization reduces width-dependent FIM sharpness at random initialization.

record.problems: Training-loss values across individual width and learning-rate settings appear only in heatmaps and are not reported numerically in the text. Figure 2 reports one trial; Figure S.2 reports the minimum across ten trials. The experiments use synthetic Gaussian inputs and teacher-generated labels, not classification benchmarks.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result rows were left out.

untested.parts: CIFAR training classification error, label corruption, and model-size or regularization effects.
Spurious local minima and the effect of adding student neurons relative to a ReLU teacher.
Training-error degradation with depth, identity shortcuts, and the stated initialization exceptions.
Initialization comparisons measuring learning speed or trainable depth.

Recovery at moderately supercritical learning rates, transient loss and curvature trajectories, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence from below the initial threshold. The reported above-threshold explosions do not distinguish moderately from excessively supercritical rates.
Faster accuracy gains, full batch normalization in the named classification settings, mini-batch SGD, and Fixup comparisons.

missing.what: The unnormalized minimum-over-ten-seeds control is plotted alongside R3 but has no row. Its gray region means loss exceeded 1000 in all ten trials; record it to make the selected-minimum comparison interpretable.
missing.locator: Supplementary Material D, Figure S.2, left panel and caption

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's limits_scope label: unmeasured accuracy speed and different benchmark settings are untested scope, not demonstrated failures. Exact heatmap values are unavailable, but explicit textual conclusions support the qualitative learning-rate comparison.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, and comparisons involving model size or regularization.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth effects on training error and identity residual shortcuts.
Comparisons of initializations for training speed or trainable depth.
Recovery above the initial linearized-model stability limit, the catapult loss trajectory, sharpness hovering at the stability threshold, and divergence below that threshold.

Accuracy-gain speed and standard batch normalization across all layers on MNIST, CIFAR-10, or ImageNet; Fixup without normalization. This study tests last-layer mean subtraction on synthetic regression training, not those classification settings.

reader_labels.reason: The authors report that mean subtraction allows larger learning rates for convergence and that the rates are independent of width (R2).
